lesson.title: Naming the Small Change: dx and dy
lesson.summary: This section shows how the differential dy = f'(x) dx formalizes linear approximation by giving separate, symbolic names to a small input change and the resulting change predicted by the tangent line.
lesson.body:
You already know that near a point, a curve can be approximated by its tangent line, and that the slope of that tangent line is written in Leibniz notation as dy/dx. The differential takes that idea and turns it into something you can compute with directly, rather than just describe geometrically. Instead of treating dy/dx only as a single symbol for "the derivative," you split it into two separate quantities, dx and dy, each meaning something on its own: dx is a chosen small change in the input, and dy is defined as f'(x) dx ,  the change in output that the tangent line predicts for that input change.

The reason this split is legitimate comes straight from linear approximation. You know that for a small change Δx, the actual change in the function, Δy = f(x+Δx) − f(x), is well approximated by f'(x)Δx. The differential simply gives that approximating expression its own name: dy = f'(x) dx. So dy is not the true change in the function ,  it's the change you'd get if the function actually were its tangent line. When dx is small, dy and the true Δy are close, and the gap between them shrinks faster than dx itself does as dx shrinks.

Take y = x². The derivative is f'(x) = 2x, so the differential is dy = 2x dx. Suppose x = 3 and you nudge it by dx = 0.1. The differential predicts dy = 2(3)(0.1) = 0.6. Now compute the actual change: Δy = (3.1)² − 3² = 9.61 − 9 = 0.61. The differential's estimate of 0.6 is very close to the true change of 0.61, off by only 0.01 ,  a small error relative to the size of the change itself. If you instead used dx = 0.01, you'd get dy = 0.06, while the true Δy = (3.01)² − 9 = 0.0601, an error of only 0.0001. The approximation gets better and better, in a very specific sense, as dx shrinks.

It helps to picture this geometrically. At the point (3, 9) on the parabola, the tangent line has slope 6. If you move along that tangent line by 0.1 in the x-direction, you rise by exactly dy = 0.6, since the tangent line is straight and its slope never changes. The actual curve, though, bends slightly upward as you move, so the true rise, 0.61, is a little more. The differential dy is literally the rise along the straight tangent line; Δy is the rise along the curve. They agree exactly only in the limit as dx → 0, but for small, finite dx they're close enough to be genuinely useful.

This is why differentials are so convenient in practice: once you know f'(x) at a point, you can estimate how the output responds to a small nudge in the input without recomputing the function from scratch, and without worrying about the curve's bending. You just multiply the derivative by dx. Later, when you study more elaborate approximation techniques and rates of change in applied problems, this same dy = f'(x) dx relationship will be the basic building block you reach for.
